source.title: Geometric Limits of Knowledge Distillation: A Minimum-Width Theorem via Superposition Theory

page_placements.theme: Distributed, redundant and compensatory contributions to behavior

record.tranche_reason: Tests the toy-model capacity/sparsity prediction using a distillation-floor measure, rather than directly measuring the original toy model’s feature geometry; also measures SAE feature structure in Pythia-410M.
record.gate_note: Toy-model prediction and sparsity results, Pythia SAE measurements, distillation floors, and linear-probe results are reported. The calculated SAE-predicted floors are not recorded as empirical measurements. The paper's cited findings from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The toy-model experiment trains narrower students on the Elhage et al. autoencoder across four sparsity levels. The observed loss floors fall with sparsity and sit well below a one-feature-per-dimension prediction. That bears indirectly on V1's sparsity-dependent packing and transition. Feature geometry is never measured. The Pythia SAE statistics are inputs to the authors' prediction pipeline, not a test of V4.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is mostly right. The authors argue that distillation floors are geometric: a student of width dS keeps at most dS·g(α) of the teacher's superposed features. On Pythia-410M, an affine fit (one free slope, baseline from the dS = 1024 run) gives R2 = 0.993. They also claim the teacher itself is in superposition (d*S ≈ 1,065 > 1,024). Coarse concepts survive compression, so the floor reflects the loss of many fine-grained tail features.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses the Elhage et al. toy autoencoder for a distillation-capacity prediction test, rather than reproducing the original superposition measurement; it also applies SAE measurements and distillation to Pythia-410M.
record.method_sensitivity: Toy-model prediction accuracy varies with sparsity; the paper says accuracy improves at higher sparsity. Pythia SAE measurements vary by layer.

fits_no_version.finding: Pythia-410M students distilled at widths 128–1024 have monotonically decreasing per-token KL floors (1.320 to 0.586 nats). The teacher-width student keeps a nonzero floor that the authors treat as an architectural baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Distillation loss floors decrease with student width and include a width-independent component.

fits_no_version.finding: Six coarse concepts stay linearly decodable at layer 12 in a dS = 128 student (mean absolute change 1.27 pp vs teacher).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Coarse concept decodability survives strong width compression.

record.problems: The paper reports a conflict for layer-8 SAE activity: §5.1 says L0 ≈ 7,400, while Table 1 reports average L0 = 234.9. The toy-model results include numerical aggregate fit statistics but many curve values are figure-only. The Pythia evidence is from one model and three SAE layers; the paper notes that the hard-cutoff approximation has approximately 5–15% error near the phase boundary and that the multilayer extension is empirically validated, not proven.

untested.parts: Feature directions, near-orthogonality and regular geometric arrangements in the toy students are never measured. Only loss floors versus width and sparsity are reported.
Not tested. Importance-ordered allocation is assumed (A2, citing Scherlis et al.), not measured. No neuron polysemanticity is measured.

SAE reconstruction fidelity and interpretability are not reported numerically. Spread of features across neurons is not measured. The 'teacher in superposition' claim follows from SAE size and L0 via a formula rather than an independent test.
Not tested. SAE features are assumed to be the model's units (a single 32× expansion).

missing.what: Universal collapse of toy floors against dS/d*S, with a sharp drop at dS = d*S. This is the sparsity-dependent transition, beyond what r4 records.
The naive formula's error degrades at high α while the refined formula's does not. Refined accuracy reaches 100% at α = 0.99.
SAE reconstruction loss per layer, which would be needed to judge whether the SAEs recover the model's features. Figure only; no numbers.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V1 limits_scope label was dropped. The 5–15% hard-cutoff error concerns the authors' approximation, not V1. The V4 labels were dropped because the SAE statistics are pipeline inputs: dictionary size is chosen, and reconstruction fidelity is not reported numerically. Internal inconsistencies weaken the Pythia numbers: layer-8 L0 is 7,400 (text) vs 234.9 (table), and feature death of 15–40% (text) conflicts with roughly 11–13% implied by Table 1. The affine fit uses four points with one free parameter. The toy-model evidence on V1 is indirect, since floors stand in for packing capacity.

versions.untested_parts: Does not directly measure pairwise feature angles, near-orthogonality, or regular geometric arrangements; it tests sparsity-dependent capacity and loss-floor predictions.
Does not measure neuron polysemanticity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions while others share.
Does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
Tests SAE-derived sparse feature measurements in one language model; does not establish that features are spread across many neurons.
Does not test SAE feature completeness, stability, or canonical status.
Does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: Elhage et al. [2022] single-layer autoencoder
rows.operation_detail: Compared predicted and actual student loss floors across 48 toy-model configurations.
rows.value: Pearson r = 0.93; MAPE = 93.9% across 140 data points; text describes prediction accuracy as above 93% at all sparsity levels.
rows.uncertainty: Actual floors shown as mean ±1 std in Figure 2; numerical error bars not stated.
rows.note: The paper reports MAPE = 93.9% while describing the result as prediction accuracy; the metric wording is retained as stated.
rows.check: This is the study's own formula's fit (Pearson r = 0.93) to the toy floors, so it is method performance. It bears on V1 only indirectly, because the formula assumes g(α)-fold packing. 'MAPE = 93.9%' is described as accuracy, so the metric is ambiguous.

source_check.correct: Pearson r = 0.93 and MAPE = 93.9% across 140 points measure the proposed formula's prediction performance. For this metric alone, state=cannot_determine and versions=none; sparsity-dependent floors and transitions are recorded separately in r3 and r4.
source_check.problem: Formula prediction performance is classified as an observed V1 effect, although it does not itself measure the representation or transition.

rows.subject: Elhage et al. [2022] single-layer autoencoder
rows.operation_detail: Compared a naive one-feature-per-dimension floor formula with actual toy-model floors.
rows.note: The paper attributes the poor R2 to systematic overestimation of absolute floor values.
rows.check: The state is wrong. The naive one-feature-per-dimension formula failing (R2 = −0.04) means actual floors are lower than a no-superposition account predicts. That is consistent with V1, not absent. The authors attribute the failure partly to systematic overestimation of absolute values. This is also a comparison between formula variants.

relationships.condition: Elhage et al. toy autoencoder, 48 configurations, α ∈ {0.80–0.99}, students dS = 1..dT
relationships.reason: Actual floors drop with higher sparsity at every width (r3). The floors are far below the one-feature-per-dimension prediction (r2) and vanish near the sparsity-dependent critical width (r1, r4). The evidence is indirect: floors, not geometry.
relationships.display_finding: Student floors fell with higher sparsity at every width, sat far below the one-feature-per-dimension prediction, and vanished near a sparsity-dependent critical width. This is indirect evidence about floors rather than about geometry.

relation.reason: The study reports its own sparsity-dependent toy loss floors and critical-width transition, bearing on V1 rather than only assuming superposition for a downstream method.

tranche.reason: Toy reconstruction floors across sparsity and width provide an indirect test of sparsity-dependent capacity and transition using a different measure from the original feature-geometry analysis.

source_check.notes:
The source reports MAPE=93.9% while also describing high prediction accuracy; retain that inconsistency rather than interpreting MAPE as accuracy.
The authors_conclusion paraphrase needs qualification: §6.3 describes fixed B=0.586, but Table 4 and Figure 7 associate R²=0.993 with fitted B=0.623. The reported 30,000-step floors are conservative upper bounds.
